A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DynaMix and retain the same principal dynamical-system and empirical forecasting benchmarks. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and redrawn material.

before.justification: V1 reports original DynaMix simulations, comparisons across 54 held-out dynamical systems, empirical time-series forecasts, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and the appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original results on the retained benchmarks, plus component ablations, Lorenz-96 experiments, nonstationary forecasting, and comparisons with custom-trained DSR models.

M1.justification: Appendix A.1 replaces the inverse-sum exploration regularizer with an averaged exponential penalty. V2 also adds a Box-Cox/detrending forecasting pipeline and an expanded-context architecture trained on nonlinear embeddings of the original training systems (A.5–A.6). These substantively extend the procedure while retaining the AL-RNN mixture and sparse teacher forcing.

E1.justification: V2 adds nonstationary Air Passengers forecasting and six-dimensional Lorenz-96 reconstruction under partial and full observation, extending important input and dynamical conditions. It also evaluates the Van-der-Pol and Rayleigh oscillators. The original 34 training systems, 54-system benchmark, Selkov example, and empirical data domains remain.

E2.justification: TimesFM joins the retained synthetic and empirical comparisons. Appendix A.7 adds reconstruction-quality comparisons against custom-trained AL-RNNs, Neural ODEs, and reservoir computers, a substantial expansion beyond TS foundation models. V1 already included a custom AL-RNN runtime reference in Figure 5, but not these quality comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported defaults change from 20 experts with M=20, P=7 to 10 experts with M=30, P=2; the initial learning rate changes from 0.002 to 0.005, and reported training sequences from 1.6 million to 0.6 million. Aggregate DS forecasting switches from endpoint error to window-averaged MASE, and empirical geometric evaluation uses 20 rather than 30 bins per dimension. Lorenz-96 introduces five-trajectory comparisons with context length 4000.

E4.justification: New Section 4.5 and Figure 9 test gating components, training-corpus diversity, training technique, and alternative expert architectures. Figure 25 adds an expert-count sweep, while the retained teacher-forcing sweep expands from geometric error alone to temporal and forecasting metrics. The existing failure examples remain as Figure 31.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly identifies standard-deviation bands or bars in Figures 3, 9, 25, and 26; v1's sensitivity bars were not defined. Benchmark summaries retain median±MAD and graphical significance annotations, but Section 4.1 drops the explicit identification of t-tests. Neither version supplies training-seed or repeated-training run counts.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the matched detailed benchmark tables contain extensively revised results. For example, DynaMix's fMRI MAE changes from 0.56 to 0.45, while cloud-request MAE changes from 147.28 to 161.58. Revised model and evaluation settings preclude interpreting these collectively as same-setting improvements. V2 adds TimesFM, Lorenz-96, ablation, and custom-model outcomes; Table 9 also replaces three previously numerical DynaMix DH entries with NaN.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 replaces rescaled inverse L1 distance between average expert usages with a similarity based on squared 2-Wasserstein distance between standardized expert weights. Appendix A.1 changes the formal forecasting-error definition, and A.6 supplies an embedding construction and dynamics-preservation argument. These are localized mathematical revisions without a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: zero-shot out-of-domain DSR without fine-tuning, preservation of long-term statistics, computational efficiency, interpretable dynamics composition, and competitive empirical forecasting. The added experiments support these existing claims. The 0.1% parameter comparison newly emphasized in the abstract already appeared in v1's conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of which architectural and training ingredients drive performance, including the relative importance of attention, CNN processing, expert type, and corpus diversity. Appendix A.7 discusses comparison fairness and possible advantages on short contexts. The limitations discussion adds decomposition-based remedies for nonstationarity and irregular-sampling considerations, while A.5 explicitly qualifies its demonstration as a proof of concept.

D1.justification: V2 adds Julia and Python code-access links and detailed custom-baseline configurations in Tables 3–5, including Neural ODE architecture, solver, and training budget. It specifies the new embedding distribution and nonstationary preprocessing procedures, and documents TimesFM evaluation access. Existing implementation information is revised, including the reported epoch time from 60 to 30 seconds.

R1.justification: The general related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain stable. Targeted additions cover LSTMs, the added oscillator and Lorenz-96 systems, Autoformer, and FEDformer; the Moirai-MoE citation is removed. TimesFM replaces Moirai in the discussion, although its underlying reference was already present in v1.

P1.justification: Most existing paragraphs and the main section sequence are retained with local wording, notation, and explanatory refinements. V2 adds an ablation subsection and three focused appendix sections, but does not extensively rewrite the existing narrative. The first-page venue statement also changes from preprint to NeurIPS 2025.

P2.justification: Numerous figures are redrawn with revised colors, axes, legends, and arrangements. Figure 5 changes from runtime bars to a parameter-count-versus-runtime scatterplot; Figure 7 changes its expert-usage display and similarity matrix presentation. Figure 8 emphasizes selected competitors, with separate appendix comparisons. New ablation and extension figures and expanded comparison/configuration tables substantially alter the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps: Section 4.5 tests the proposed model's components, and Appendix A.7 establishes direct comparisons with methods designed for DSR. These substantially strengthen assessment of why DynaMix works and how its reconstruction quality compares. Dimensional-generalization experiments and code links further improve support and reproducibility. Unexplained NaNs in Table 9 and inconsistent MAE/MASE labeling limit clarity, but do not outweigh these central gains.
